title: "Put yourself on the map"
subtitle: "Geospatial visualization with R · beginner exercise (5 minutes)"
format: live-html
engine: knitr

{{< include _extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

R runs right here in your browser. You do not need to install anything. Press **Run Code** and a world map appears.

## Your mission

1. Press **Run Code**. You see the world, **Zealandia** in turquoise, and three places.
2. Change **"Chennai"** and its two numbers to **your hometown** (cheat list below). Run again: your place appears on the map.
3. Change `"red"` to another colour, for example `"orange"`, `"gold"` or `"hotpink"`.
4. Add a fourth place: add a comma and one new value inside each `c( ... )`.

```{webr}
.w <- strsplit(strsplit(WORLD_TXT, "|", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], ";", fixed = TRUE)
.world <- lapply(.w, function(p) { xy <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(p, ",", fixed = TRUE)); list(x = as.numeric(xy[, 1]), y = as.numeric(xy[, 2])) })
.zx <- c(160,164,169,172,175,179,183,185,184,178,167,165,167,166,162,159,160)
.zy <- c(-22,-19,-20,-25,-31,-36,-41,-46,-50,-54,-55,-50,-45,-40,-35,-29,-22)
draw_world <- function(main = "My map") {
  par(mar = c(2.2, 2.6, 2.4, .6), bg = "#06182b", fg = "#9fb6c8", col.axis = "#9fb6c8", col.lab = "#9fb6c8", col.main = "white")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 360), ylim = c(-62, 80), asp = 1, xlab = "", ylab = "", axes = FALSE)
  rect(-10, -90, 370, 90, col = "#0f4c81", border = NA)
  abline(v = seq(0, 360, 30), h = seq(-60, 80, 20), col = rgb(1, 1, 1, .12), lwd = .6)
  for (p in .world) polygon(p$x, p$y, col = "#9bd17a", border = "#3f7d3f", lwd = .4)
  polygon(.zx, .zy, col = rgb(.05, .95, .8, .55), border = "#0fffd0", lwd = 2.2)
  text(172, -59.5, "ZEALANDIA", col = "#0fffd0", font = 2, cex = .9)
  axis(1, at = seq(0, 360, 60), labels = c("0", "60E", "120E", "180", "120W", "60W", "0"), tick = FALSE, line = -.8, cex.axis = .8)
  axis(2, at = seq(-60, 80, 20), labels = paste0(abs(seq(-60, 80, 20)), c(rep("S", 3), "", rep("N", 4))), tick = FALSE, las = 1, line = -.8, cex.axis = .8)
  title(main = main, line = .6)
}
add_places <- function(places, col = "red") {
  points(places$lon, places$lat, pch = 21, bg = col, col = "white", cex = 1.8, lwd = 1.5)
  for (dx in c(-.5, .5)) for (dy in c(-.5, .5)) text(places$lon + dx, places$lat + 4.5 + dy, places$name, col = "black", cex = .85, font = 2)
  text(places$lon, places$lat + 4.5, places$name, col = "white", cex = .85, font = 2)
}

```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_map
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
# 1) Your places: name, longitude (east-west), latitude (north-south)
cities <- data.frame(
  name = c("Cologne", "Wellington", "Chennai"),
  lon  = c(6.96, 174.78, 80.27),
  lat  = c(50.94, -41.29, 13.08)
)

# 2) Draw the world map (Zealandia is the turquoise shape)
draw_world()

# 3) Put your places on the map. Change the colour here!
add_places(cities, col = "red")
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_map"}
Replace `"Chennai"`, `80.27` and `13.08` with a place from the cheat list. Keep the quotation marks around the name.
:::

::: { .hint exercise="ex_map"}
To add a place, put a comma after the last value in each list. For example `name = c("Cologne", "Wellington", "Chennai", "Paris")`, then add the matching longitude and latitude.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_map" }
```r
cities <- data.frame(
  name = c("Cologne", "Wellington", "Mumbai", "Paris"),
  lon  = c(6.96, 174.78, 72.88, 2.35),
  lat  = c(50.94, -41.29, 19.08, 48.86)
)
draw_world()
add_places(cities, col = "orange")
```
:::

## Cheat list

| Place | lon | lat |
|---|---|---|
| Cologne | 6.96 | 50.94 |
| Berlin | 13.40 | 52.52 |
| Paris | 2.35 | 48.86 |
| London | 359.87 | 51.51 |
| Chennai | 80.27 | 13.08 |
| Mumbai | 72.88 | 19.08 |
| Wellington | 174.78 | -41.29 |
| Auckland | 174.76 | -36.85 |
| New York | 285.94 | 40.71 |

Longitude is counted from 0 to 360 so that Zealandia, which crosses the date line, stays in one piece. For other places, search "[city] coordinates". If the longitude is negative (west), add 360.

## What you just did

You turned numbers (longitude and latitude) into a **map**. `draw_world()` and `add_places()` are ready-made helpers; inside they use the same few R ideas from the overview page (lists, tables, `plot`, `polygon`, `text`). This is geospatial visualization: the same idea businesses use to plot stores, customers and deliveries.
